From Cabinet to governor: Ruku’s City Hall gamble
items.description: UDA Nairobi ticket turning into a contest between Public Service CS and Kasarani MP Karauri.
content: Public Service Cabinet Secretary Geoffrey Ruku during an interview at his office at Harambee House, Nairobi on November 11, 2026.

The battle for the United Democratic Alliance (UDA) ticket in Nairobi is emerging as an early test of President William Ruto’s ability to manage competing political ambitions within his own party, with two high-profile aspirants seeking to succeed Governor Johnson Sakaja and both positioning themselves around the Head of State.

Public Service Cabinet Secretary Geoffrey Ruku and Kasarani MP Ronald Karauri have declared interest in the August 2027 governorship contest, setting up a potentially difficult nomination battle for a party seeking to reclaim City Hall following Mr Sakaja’s defection to the Orange Democratic Movement (ODM).

On Saturday, Mr Ruku officially launched his bid at the UDA Party headquarters, where he was received by a section of party officials and other grassroots leaders. He was also accompanied by UDA ward representatives in Nairobi.
Public Service Cabinet Secretary Geoffrey Ruku gestures during an interview at his office at Harambee House, Nairobi on November 11, 2026.

He has presented himself as an experienced administrator capable of transforming the capital. Mr Karauri is seeking to build a citywide campaign from his parliamentary base in Kasarani, backed by a reception at UDA headquarters that brought together some of the party’s senior figures.

The emerging rivalry is complicated by the competing claims of presidential support. Mr Karauri was welcomed into UDA by National Assembly Majority Leader Kimani Ichung’wah and UDA Secretary-General Hassan Omar, with Mr Ichung’wah revealing that President Ruto had personally called him to facilitate the legislator’s reception into the party. Both leaders were, however, absent when Mr Ruku launched his bid at the party headquarters.

Mr Ruku said his decision to contest on the UDA ticket was informed by his association with the President’s leadership, although he has been reluctant to discuss whether he has held direct conversations with the Head of State about the matter.

“I identify with UDA, though I was elected to Parliament on the Democratic Party. The Head of State has transformed this country and I fully identify with UDA ideals. The transformation that we want to achieve in Nairobi and impact can only be achieved through UDA,” he said.
Read: Battle for City Hall: Inside Nairobi’s high-stakes governor seat
Asked whether he had consulted the President about his transition from the Cabinet to City Hall, Mr Ruku told the Daily Nation, “Let’s leave the President out of the discussions.”

The competing ambitions expose a dilemma for the ruling party on how to accommodate two politicians who both want to be its face in Nairobi without creating divisions that could undermine its efforts to regain the county’s top seat.
Mr Sakaja’s departure has created an opening for UDA, but the party’s attempt to capitalise on it is already facing internal competition over who should inherit its political machinery.
Nairobi Governor Johnson Sakaja addresses ODM supporters during a mega rally in memory of Raila Odinga at Jacaranda Grounds on October 31, 2026.

Mr Karauri’s entry into UDA on November 9 was accompanied by a public show of support from senior party officials, raising questions about whether the event was simply a welcome ceremony or an early indication of the party leadership’s preferred candidate.

Mr Ichung’wah welcomed the legislator and described him as the party’s candidate to challenge ODM in Nairobi, remarks that appeared to place Mr Karauri ahead of other aspirants who had already expressed interest in the ticket.

Mr Ruku has already hit the ground running and is already building a grassroots machinery that will help him capture the seat. He has held public participation meetings in South B, Kasarani and Woodley before the launch on Saturday.
“I have lived in this city since I was 18 years old. My children, all of them, have been born in this city, five of them. My children go to school in this city,” he said.
Read: UDA vs ODM: Intrigues of Sakaja, Karauri gamble in Nairobi battle
He added that having lived in different parts of Nairobi, he understands the challenges confronting residents in both established estates and informal settlements.

“Whether you are living in Kawangware, or in Doonholm, or in whatever corner of the city, these are problems which can be taken care of, if we get it right as far as the leadership of the city is concerned,” he said.

He is also questioning Mr Karauri’s development record in Kasarani and his contribution to Parliament. The Cabinet Secretary argued that the MP should first demonstrate what he has achieved in his constituency before seeking a bigger political office.
He claimed that residents of Kasarani were dissatisfied with Mr Karauri’s performance and questioned whether the legislator could secure another parliamentary term.
“Go to Kasarani and ask people who live in Kasarani whether they can vote him back as a member of parliament and they will tell you a big no,” he said.
Mr Ruku further accused the legislator of seeking the gubernatorial seat as an escape route from his constituency’s political challenges.
Read: Kasarani MP Ronald Karauri joins UDA, eyes Nairobi governor seat
“Running for a senior position cannot be an escape route to run away from your misdeed and to run away from your omission or errors of omission or commission,” he said.

Mr Ruku is positioning himself as an experienced administrator who can transfer his national government experience to the management of Nairobi, citing his time as Mbeere North MP and his current Cabinet position.
“I can manage a ministry which covers the entire Republic of Kenya,” he said, arguing that the experience has prepared him to manage the complex affairs of the capital.

Mr Karauri, on the other hand, brings parliamentary experience from Kasarani and a business background, while his reception at UDA headquarters has given his entry public visibility among the party’s senior leadership.
The biggest challenge for UDA could be managing the ambitions of its aspirants without triggering defections or independent candidacies.
Mr Ruku has already indicated that he is prepared to accept the outcome of a competitive nomination process, even if Mr Karauri emerges as the party’s candidate.
Kasarani Member of Parliament Ronald Karauri.
“If we go for nominations and I am not successful, I accept and I will support whoever will win the nominations for UDA,” he said.

Mr Karauri, however, has also signalled that he is determined to appear on the ballot, saying he could pursue an independent candidature if he believes the party’s nomination process has been manipulated.

“I’m hoping that we will have a transparent nomination process. When we get to around March next year when the nominations are done, in case again I’m played like I was done in Jubilee Party, then I will run as an independent candidate,” Mr Karauri said, adding that he must be on the ballot by all means possible.
Unlike CS Ruku, who declared that he would support the winner of the nominations, Mr Karauri maintained that his minimum requirement will be to be on the ballot, where voters would decide his fate.

Development Is Not Charity: Taxation, Patronage and the Politics of Power in Kenya
items.description: Development is not a presidential gift; it is a public obligation funded by the labour and taxes of the people. Yet Kenya’s political landscape increasingly presents public development as the personal…
content: Development is not a presidential gift; it is a public obligation funded by the labour and taxes of the people. Yet Kenya’s political landscape increasingly presents public development as the personal generosity of President William Ruto, who travels across the country announcing projects in ways that often blur the distinction between public responsibility and electoral mobilisation.

From a historical materialist perspective, this is not merely a question of political rhetoric but of power, ownership and the distribution of public resources. The state collects taxes from workers, peasants, traders and businesses across the country. These resources are pooled into the national treasury and must serve the collective needs of the population, not the electoral interests of an individual or political faction.

Walter Rodney, in his final speech, Sign of the Times, delivered on 6 June 1980, challenged the separation of material needs from political rights. His argument that access to milk and constitutional freedom were inseparable reminds us that material conditions and political power are interconnected. In Kenya, access to roads, hospitals, water, schools and electricity cannot be reduced to presidential generosity; these are necessities financed through collective taxation and owed to the people.

The politics of announcing projects during presidential tours risks reproducing a patronage system in which communities are encouraged to associate public investment with political loyalty. Development then becomes a political currency, used to cultivate support, consolidate power and influence electoral outcomes. This obscures the fact that taxpayers are financing these projects in the first place.

The contradiction is particularly glaring in a country where taxation continues to burden ordinary citizens amid rising living costs. Workers and small businesses contribute to the public purse, yet they are often politically positioned as beneficiaries of the very resources they collectively generate. Such a narrative reinforces the illusion that development flows from the generosity of political leaders rather than from the productive labour and financial contributions of society.

Development should not be a reward for voting for the ruling party, attending presidential rallies or endorsing a re-election campaign. It must be guided by public need, equitable distribution, transparency and democratic accountability.
The struggle, therefore, is not simply over which region receives a road or a water project. It is about challenging the politics of patronage that turns public obligations into political favours.
The President is not the benefactor of the people; he is the custodian of public resources. Development is not charity. It is the people’s right.

Wachira Nyaga is a cadre of the Revolutionary Socialist League, a Founding Member of Social Justice Movement Kenya, a member of Kenya Organic Intellectuals, and the Founder of Embu Community Justice Center. His work focuses on political education, community organising, social justice, African liberation, and the relationship between theory and practice.

10 Most Financially Stable SACCOS to Trust with Your Savings, New Report
items.description: SASRA’s 2025 report ranks Kenya’s deposit-taking Saccos for financial stability, showing how Winas and Newfortis rival sector giants on key financial metrics.
content: PAY ATTENTION: Mark TUKO.co.ke as a preferred source, and our content will appear higher in your Google feed!

The Sacco Societies Regulatory Authority (SASRA) has published its SACCO Supervision Annual Report 2025 , released on October 6, ranking Kenya's Deposit-Taking Saccos (DT-Saccos) across a range of financial health indicators.
PAY ATTENTION: TUKO is in WhatsApp Channels now! Subscribe and read news in your favourite messenger.

The report measures five core metrics: Core Capital to Total Assets (CCA), Core Capital to Total Deposits (CCD), Institutional Capital to Total Assets (ICA), external borrowing levels, and Non-Performing Loan (NPL) ratios. Based on these indicators, the following ten institutions stand out as the most financially stable.
Winas DT-Sacco leads the rankings, posting a CCD ratio of 84.94% against the regulatory minimum of 8%, alongside a CCA of 42.22%, zero external borrowing, and an NPL ratio of just 1.61%.

Kenya National Police (KNP) DT-Sacco, the third-largest by total assets, follows closely with a CCA of 35.67%, an ICA of 30.11%, no external debt, and an NPL of 2.33%.
Transnation DT-Sacco ranks third, meeting all capital thresholds comfortably with a CCA of 21.10% and an NPL of 2.90%, while Hazina DT-Sacco records a CCA of 16.15% and an NPL ratio of just 2.00%.
Sheria DT-Sacco, which serves Kenya's legal fraternity, maintains a CCA of 18.17% and zero external borrowing, with NPLs at 2.80%.
Newfortis DT-Sacco distinguishes itself with the lowest NPL ratio on the entire list at 0.48%, supported by a CCA of 13.48% and no external debt.
Imarisha DT-Sacco records a CCA of 17.49% and an NPL of 1.53%, with minimal external borrowing of 2.44%.

Mwalimu National DT-Sacco, the largest Sacco in Kenya by total assets, improved its NPL ratio to 2.42% in 2025, reinforcing confidence in the teachers' institution. Its CCA stands at 13.96% and ICA at 9.89%.
Stima DT-Sacco, the second-largest, holds a CCA of 19.22% and an ICA of 12.84%.
KCB’s KSh 58.6b profit: What it means for your loan, hustle, job prospects
Its NPL ratio of 6.48% is higher than others on the list, though the institution carries negligible external borrowing at 1.39%.
Unison DT-Sacco rounds out the top ten with a CCA of 16.15%, zero external debt, and an NPL of 2.16%.
A consistent pattern across the top performers is the near-total absence of external borrowing, with most institutions relying entirely on member deposits.
The report also highlights that NPL ratios below 3% serve as a reliable indicator of responsible lending practices.

SASRA's data further underscores that financial stability does not correlate directly with size, as smaller institutions such as Winas and Newfortis outperform some of the sector's largest players on key capital and asset-quality metrics.
SASRA warned that SACCO members should look beyond high dividends and consider their institution’s financial health .
The regulator cautioned that excessive payouts could weaken a SACCO’s ability to lend, withstand unexpected losses and protect members’ savings.

Govt urges cooperative societies to embrace reforms to drive growth
items.description: The government has called on cooperative societies across the country to embrace reforms, digitalisation, professional management and innovation to strengthen
content: The government has called on cooperative societies across the country to embrace reforms, digitalisation, professional management and innovation to strengthen their contribution to Kenya’s economic growth and wealth creation.

Principal Secretary (PS) for the State Department for Cooperatives, Patrick Kilemi, said cooperatives must move beyond traditional savings mobilisation and agricultural produce aggregation to become commercially competitive enterprises capable of investing, processing, manufacturing and accessing local and international markets.

Speaking during the Fifth Annual Cabinet Secretary’s Consultative Forum for Cooperatives and Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) held from November 16 to 20, 2026, at Sawela Lodge in Naivasha, Kilemi said cooperatives were central to the government’s Bottom-Up Economic Transformation Agenda (BETA).

He noted that the cooperative movement had the membership base, reach and institutional capacity to mobilise domestic resources, attract investment, create employment, promote financial inclusion and connect millions of Kenyans to economic opportunities.

Kilemi challenged cooperative leaders to rethink their business models and embrace modern approaches that would enhance productivity, competitiveness and sustainability. In his view, the success of the cooperative movement should not be measured by the number of registered societies but by the economic value they create and the impact they have on the lives of their members.

Kilemi said significant progress had been made on the Cooperatives Bill, 2024, which is expected to strengthen governance, accountability and supervision within the sector. Preparatory work on the regulations required to support its implementation is also underway.
The hidden profit gap facing Kenya’s women in agribusiness

In the Saccos subsector, the government is advancing proposals for a Central Liquidity Facility and shared services framework aimed at strengthening financial stability, institutional resilience and operational efficiency.

Furthermore, the Kenya Cooperative Transformation Strategy has progressed, with its first draft undergoing stakeholder consultations to provide a long-term roadmap for modernising and improving the competitiveness of cooperative enterprises.

On digital transformation, Kilemi said the implementation of the Cooperative Management Information System was at an advanced stage, adding that the system would improve transparency, accountability, data management, registration and supervision of cooperative societies.

In the agricultural sector, the government continues to position cooperatives at the centre of strategic value chains, including coffee, dairy, livestock and cotton, with emphasis on increasing production, processing, value addition and market access.

Kilemi emphasised that the ongoing reforms were not intended merely to improve the administration of cooperative societies but to fundamentally change how they conduct business and contribute to the national economy.

The PS urged cooperative leaders and members to view the reforms as opportunities to address longstanding institutional weaknesses, strengthen their organisations and unlock new economic opportunities.

He called on cooperatives to invest in modern processing facilities, develop their own brands, establish strategic partnerships and explore international markets to ensure members benefit from greater value addition.
Saccos were also challenged to embrace technology, strengthen their financial systems and expand their role in supporting enterprise development through competitive financial services.
According to Kilemi, professionalisation, digitalisation, good governance, innovation and strategic partnerships would be critical in building strong and sustainable cooperative institutions.
Kilemi reaffirmed the government’s commitment to creating an enabling policy, legal and institutional environment to support the transformation of the cooperative movement.
He urged cooperative leaders to take ownership of the reform agenda and work closely with the government and development partners to reposition the sector as a major driver of economic growth.

Besides, he noted that the cooperative movement had played a significant role in Kenya’s economic development for generations but needed to adopt greater ambition, innovation and competitiveness to remain relevant in the changing business environment.
Station wagon registrations drop 17.2pc in Kenya

The Principal Secretary called on stakeholders to work collectively in implementing the reforms, stressing that the future of the sector would depend on their willingness to embrace change and move beyond traditional business practices.
Finally, he urged the cooperative movement to actively participate in shaping the country’s economic future rather than remain spectators to the ongoing transformation.

The forum brought together stakeholders in the cooperative and MSME sectors to deliberate on reforms, challenges and opportunities for strengthening the sectors’ contribution to Kenya’s economic transformation.

William Ruto Secretly Travels To Congo Amid Strained Kenya-DRC Relations
items.description: President William Ruto travelled to Oyo for talks initiated by Denis Sassou Nguesso, amid strained Kenya-DRC ties, with Félix Tshisekedi expected to attend.
content: PAY ATTENTION: TUKO is in WhatsApp Channels now! Subscribe and read news in your favourite messenger.
Nancy Odindo is a Current Affairs Editor at TUKO.co.ke, covering political and world news. Odindo has over six years of journalism experience and joined TUKO.co.ke in 2023.
President William Ruto has travelled to Oyo, in the Republic of Congo, to attend a high-level four-party meeting convened by Congolese President Denis Sassou Nguesso.
The Congo government announced on Sunday, November 21, that Ruto had arrived in Oyo to participate in the gathering, which was described as a high-level diplomatic engagement initiated by Nguesso.

According to Congolese media reports, the meeting is also expected to bring together Democratic Republic of Congo President Félix Tshisekedi and Togolese Prime Minister Faure Gnassingbé, though no official confirmation of the full attendee list had been issued at the time of publication.
Ruto is reported to have left Kenya through Kisumu International Airport on Saturday after concluding a series of engagements with residents during a tour of Western Kenya .
The departure attracted attention given the low-profile nature of the trip and the diplomatic sensitivities surrounding Kenya-DRC relations.

The meeting takes place against the backdrop of a difficult period in relations between Nairobi and Kinshasa. Tensions first escalated in December 2023 when the Alliance Fleuve Congo (AFC), a political-military coalition linked to the M23 rebel movement, held a launch event in Nairobi.
The DRC government objected strongly, accusing Kenya of providing a platform to a group it regards as hostile. Kenya maintained that it had no legal basis to prevent freedom of political expression.

The relationship deteriorated further in October 2025 when Nairobi hosted a political meeting attended by Congolese opposition figures, among them former DRC President Joseph Kabila, drawing fresh criticism from Kinshasa.
The specific agenda of the Oyo meeting has not been officially disclosed, but its timing and composition suggest it is aimed at addressing regional security and diplomatic tensions involving the DRC.

items.title: Kenyans Saddened After KSh 6.5m BMW Z4 With KEA Plate Is Spotted at Salvage Yard
items.description: Photos of a KSh 6.5 million BMW Z4 bearing a KEA number plate at a salvage yard have sparked reactions in Kenya, with many wondering whether the owner survived.

A luxury car that would ordinarily turn heads on Nairobi's roads has become a subject of online discussion after images emerged showing it parked at a salvage yard.
The vehicle, a BMW Z4 bearing a Kenyan KEA registration number, caught the attention of social media users after posts showing it at the yard circulated online.
The images were shared by several social media platforms, prompting reactions from Kenyans who expressed sadness at the sight of the high-end convertible.

The BMW Z4 is a luxury sports car known for its sleek design, two-seat configuration and convertible roof, making it a distinctive vehicle on Kenyan roads.

Recent listings for BMW Z4 models on Kenyan car marketplaces indicate that some versions can command prices in the region of KSh 6.5 million, depending on their model year, condition and specifications.
For many social media users, seeing such an expensive vehicle at a salvage yard was particularly striking, with some expressing disbelief that a car of its value could end up in such a location.
Many were concerned that a vehicle with that registration must be newly registered in Kenya, which means the owner didn't get more than six months to enjoy it
The images, however, did not provide an explanation of what had happened to the vehicle.
It was also not immediately clear where the salvage yard was located, how long the BMW had been there or whether it had sustained accident damage.
There was no confirmed information indicating whether the vehicle was an insurance write-off, awaiting repairs, undergoing assessment or being kept at the yard for another reason.
The circumstances surrounding the BMW's appearance therefore remain unclear, even as its photographs continue to attract attention online.

Seven Kenyan Counties Present Sustainable Cooling Projects for Investment
items.description: Projects span cold chains, healthcare refrigeration, dairy cooling and efficient buildings as SEforALL launches a finance-readiness guide.
content: Projects span cold chains, healthcare refrigeration, dairy cooling and efficient buildings as SEforALL launches a finance-readiness guide.

Seven counties in Kenya presented sustainable cooling projects to government officials, development partners, technology providers and industry representatives at the Sustainable Cooling Marketplace in Kisumu. The event, organized in collaboration with the County Government of Kisumu and supported by Sustainable Energy for All (SEforALL), also marked the launch of SEforALL’s Investment Prospectus Guide for Heat and Cooling Action Plans.

Representatives from Homa Bay, Kilifi, Kisumu, Makueni, Nakuru, Taita Taveta and Tana River identified seven potential projects covering agricultural and fisheries cold chains, healthcare refrigeration, dairy cooling and energy-efficient buildings. Proposed installations include solar-powered ice-making plants, fish cold rooms, solar cold storage for fishing communities and a vegetable packhouse with 15 tonnes (approximately 16.5 US tons) of cold storage capacity for African leafy vegetables.

Other proposals include six solar-powered milk-chilling plants, new and replacement vaccine refrigerators and cold chain equipment for healthcare facilities, and the replacement of air conditioners in 30 public classrooms with high-efficiency units. Counties also proposed passive cooling measures, green building design and urban cooling interventions.

The Investment Prospectus Guide provides a five-step process for developing finance-ready projects, covering project definition, stakeholder engagement, costing, financing scenarios, investment documentation and connections with financing partners. Potential funding sources include public budgets, grants, concessional finance and blended finance. Participants identified limited technical capacity, insufficient data and project preparation requirements as key barriers to securing investment.

Kenya’s National Cooling Action Plan, launched in 2023, prioritizes energy-efficient cooling appliances, low-global-warming-potential refrigerants and expanded access to sustainable cooling, including agricultural cold chains. William Melau, Assistant Coordinator of the National Ozone Unit at the Ministry of Environment, Climate Change and Forestry, also highlighted solar-powered cooling, passive cooling and Kenya’s commitments under the Kigali Amendment. SEforALL plans to continue supporting counties in identifying priority projects and engaging potential financiers.

Engineers blame corruption and regulatory gaps for Kenya’s building collapses
items.description: The Institution of Engineering Technology of Kenya has called on President William Ruto to urgently address what it describes as serious regulatory gaps fuelling a dangerous rise in building collapses across the country, warning that corruption and government inaction are placing ordinary Kenyans at risk.
content: IET-K calls on President Ruto to act as professionals warn that weak oversight is costing lives

The Institution of Engineering Technology of Kenya has called on President William Ruto to urgently address what it describes as serious regulatory gaps fuelling a dangerous rise in building collapses across the country, warning that corruption and government inaction are placing ordinary Kenyans at risk.

Speaking at the 6th IET-K Annual Conference in Mombasa on Saturday, more than 700 engineering professionals expressed alarm at the government’s failure to operationalise key regulatory bodies responsible for overseeing the construction sector. The gathering underscored the growing frustration within the profession over a crisis that has claimed lives and shaken public confidence in Kenya’s built environment.

IET-K President Bibiye Mahmoud Juma told delegates that critical institutions — among them the Kenya Engineering Technology Registration Board, the Engineers Board of Kenya, and the Board of Quantity Surveyors and Architects — have yet to be fully constituted, leaving the industry without the professional oversight it urgently needs. Juma urged Ruto to take personal responsibility for ensuring those bodies are properly established and empowered to function. She also called on the Cabinet Secretary in charge of Roads and the National Construction Authority to enforce proper regulation of professionals working on construction sites across the country.

Engineer Lawrence Michemi was blunt in his assessment, describing corruption as the single greatest obstacle to improving safety standards in the industry. He argued that existing loopholes in the regulatory system make it far too easy for individuals to engage in corrupt practices — and that until those gaps are closed, no amount of goodwill will be sufficient. Michemi also stressed the need to build a genuine culture of safety in society, and called for greater use of technology to promote discipline, improve efficiency and strengthen supervision on construction sites.

The warnings come against a backdrop of mounting public anxiety over building collapses, which have become an increasingly visible safety emergency in Kenya. Each incident raises fresh questions about the quality of construction materials, the adequacy of professional supervision, and whether approved building standards are being followed at all.

Professor Michael Saulo, Dean at the Technical University of Mombasa, used the platform to draw attention to the often-overlooked contribution of technicians and technologists in the construction process. While engineers design structures, Saulo explained, it is technicians and technologists who implement those designs on the ground and ensure that the work meets required standards — a distinction that matters enormously when things go wrong.

The conference put forward several concrete proposals. These included declaring building collapses a national disaster, developing clear action plans to improve public safety, strengthening risk management practices across the industry, and accelerating the adoption of technology and innovation to reduce opportunities for corruption and improve monitoring of construction projects.

The professionals were emphatic that lasting change will require more than reacting after buildings fall. They want the government to rebuild regulatory institutions from the ground up, enforce genuine accountability, and ensure that only qualified professionals are permitted to oversee construction work. As pressure on the government intensifies, Kenyans are looking for solutions that go beyond the emergency response — solutions that will protect lives, restore public trust, and guarantee that every structure built in this country is safe to enter.
The message from Mombasa was clear: the safety of buildings must never be sacrificed for financial gain, and the time for half-measures has long passed.

Kenya’s new cancer rules set treatment deadlines and track SHA cover
items.description: The rules add treatment deadlines and digital tracking, but the reports leave enforcement and the system’s rollout unclear.
content: The rules add treatment deadlines and digital tracking, but the reports leave enforcement and the system’s rollout unclear.

Kenya’s 2026 cancer guidelines set deadlines for diagnosis and treatment and link cancer care to a digital system intended to track use of the Ksh800,000 SHA oncology benefit . The Ministry of Health says the rules will standardise care and improve accountability; patients have complained that delayed approvals and hospital charges can leave them without cover before treatment is complete.

The guidelines are the first major revision of Kenya’s cancer treatment protocols since 2019 . Under the new timelines, adults should receive a diagnosis within 60 days of first contact with a healthcare provider, and children within 30 days. After diagnosis, patients should be assessed at a designated or specialised cancer treatment centre within 14 days and start treatment within 31 days of registration.

The timelines are intended to cut waits across consultations, testing and referrals. The reports do not say how compliance will be measured, or what consequences facilities will face if patients miss those deadlines.

Cancer treatment will be connected to SHA’s digital oncology module. The system is intended to create a unified patient record that can be accessed across facilities, reducing duplicate records and helping care continue when patients move between hospitals. Health Cabinet Secretary Aden Duale said it would also improve coordination and management of the oncology benefit.

Patients have raised concerns that the Ksh800,000 allocation is exhausted before treatment ends, as well as about delayed approvals, inflated bills and procedures they consider unnecessary. One patient quoted by People Daily described waiting at hospital while approval remained pending. SHA Chairman Abdi Mohamed said the authority had received complaints about questionable charges, including consultations allegedly billed when no doctor was present.

The Ministry and SHA have warned contracted facilities against using up a patient’s allocation on unnecessary services or billing for care that was not provided. The government says facilities must account for their charges. The reports do not explain how patients can challenge a bill or secure treatment when a disagreement over charges or approval arises.

The revised guidelines include molecular profiling, targeted therapy and immunotherapy—approaches the reports say were not widely embedded in the 2019 protocols. Molecular profiling examines a tumour’s genetic characteristics to help guide treatment; targeted therapy acts on particular abnormalities in cancer cells, while immunotherapy helps the immune system recognise and fight cancer.

The two People Daily accounts give slightly different estimates of the annual cancer burden: one says more than 44,000 new cases , the other says nearly 45,000. Both describe cancer as a major and growing burden. Neither provides a breakdown by cancer type, county or access to the newer treatments.

There is also no implementation timetable in the reports, nor a named body responsible for checking whether hospitals meet the new deadlines. A unified record and clearer rules may help, but the coverage does not establish whether the digital module is already operating or how quickly facilities will be connected.

Only People Daily’s account is available here, so there is no reporting from another outlet to compare against. Its two reports overlap substantially; the longer account adds direct remarks from Duale, Mohamed and a patient. The next test is whether the deadlines and billing safeguards change what patients experience at facilities—not just what the guidelines prescribe.

items.title: ADVANCING CRITICAL CARE EXPERTISE FOR MILITARY HEALTHCARE EXCELLENCE
items.description: ADVANCING CRITICAL CARE EXPERTISE FOR MILITARY HEALTHCARE EXCELLENCE Ministry of Defence – Kenya
content: Specialised medical expertise is vital to saving lives, improving patient outcomes and sustaining operational readiness within the Kenya Defence Forces (KDF). As military healthcare demands continue to evolve, investment in advanced clinical training remains essential to developing a skilled, responsive and professionally competent healthcare workforce.

The Defence College of Health Sciences (DCHS), a College of the National Defence University-Kenya (NDU-K), officially opened the November 2026 cohort of the Higher Diploma in Kenya Registered Critical Care Nursing (HDCCN) programme, marking another milestone in advancing specialised nursing education within the Defence Forces.

The programme is designed to equip nursing personnel with advanced clinical knowledge, specialised competencies and practical skills essential for managing critically ill patients and delivering high-quality care in demanding healthcare environments.

Through the training, participants will enhance their professional proficiency in critical care nursing, contributing to improved patient management, clinical decision-making and the delivery of specialised medical services across military healthcare facilities.

Beyond individual professional development, the programme represents a strategic investment in institutional healthcare capacity, ensuring that the KDF maintains a pool of highly trained medical personnel capable of responding to complex healthcare needs in both operational and non-operational settings.
The initiative reflects DCHS’s central role in advancing medical education, professional excellence and specialised healthcare training within the Defence Forces.

By investing in critical care expertise, the KDF continues to build a resilient, competent and future-ready military healthcare system capable of safeguarding the health of its personnel and delivering quality medical services to those under its care.
